name: Score-Based Generative Model
analogy: Think of it as a hiker lost in fog on a hilly landscape where the high ground is realistic market data. At every spot the model gives a small arrow pointing uphill toward more realistic data. To make something new, start at a random spot and keep following the arrows, with a little shaking, until you stand on a believable hilltop.

steps.title: Blur the real data with several noise levels
steps.description: Real samples are corrupted with random noise at many different strengths, from a whisper to a roar. Heavy noise hides almost everything and light noise leaves the data nearly intact.
steps.inExample: A real 20-bar window of normalized 5-minute returns is blurred at 10 noise levels, from faint to overwhelming.

steps.title: Train a network to point toward cleaner data
steps.description: The network is shown a noisy sample and the noise level and learns to output an arrow: the direction in which the sample would look more like real data. This arrow is what the model calls the score.
steps.inExample: Shown a noisy window at a medium noise level, the network outputs an arrow telling each of the 20 values how to move to look more realistic.

steps.title: Learn arrows at every noise level
steps.description: At heavy noise the arrows describe broad structure, and at light noise they describe fine detail. Covering all levels lets the model guide a sample from pure static all the way to a clean result.
steps.inExample: The network gives broad-shape arrows at the noisiest level and small-correction arrows at the faintest level.

steps.title: Start from pure static
steps.description: To generate, you begin with a sample of pure random noise, the foggiest starting point, and the highest noise level.
steps.inExample: The start is 20 random values with no market structure at all.

steps.title: Walk uphill with a little shaking
steps.description: At each step the sample is moved a small distance along the arrow, and a little fresh noise is added so that it explores rather than rushing to one spot. The noise level is lowered gradually as the walk continues.
steps.inExample: Over 100 steps the 20 values move along the arrows while the noise level falls from heavy to faint.

steps.title: Read off the finished sample
steps.description: When the noise level reaches its lowest value, the sample is a new data point that resembles the real ones. The same arrows can also clean a partially noisy real sample or flag one that sits far from realistic regions.
steps.inExample: The 20 values now form a window of returns with a realistic mix of small moves and one larger drop.

useFor.task: Generating synthetic windows of market data
useFor.example: Producing new 20-bar windows of normalized 5-minute MNQ returns to widen the scenarios a strategy is tested on.
Starting from a feature row with corrupted values, such as a bad volume print, and nudging it back toward the realistic region.

useFor.task: Checking whether a window is unusual
useFor.example: Looking at how large the arrow is for a given window; a very large arrow means the window sits far from the realistic regions.

avoidWhen: You need an answer fast; generation takes many small steps, so simpler models such as a variational autoencoder or a generative adversarial network respond far quicker.
You need a calibrated next-bar probability; a model trained on that target directly is more suitable than one that learns the whole data shape.

example.scenario: A researcher trained a score-based model on 20-bar windows of normalized 5-minute MNQ returns. They want a new synthetic window, and they also want to know how far one real window sits from the realistic region.

input.summary: A starting sample of pure noise and the settings of the walk.

fields.name: window length
fields.meaning: How many values are in each sample, one per 5-minute bar.

fields.name: starting sample
fields.meaning: The pure noise that the walk starts from.

fields.name: noise levels
fields.meaning: The ladder of noise strengths the walk steps down through.

fields.name: steps per noise level
fields.meaning: How many small uphill moves are made before the noise level is lowered.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The scale used to turn normalized returns back into points on the chart.

output.summary: A finished synthetic window and a check on how realistic it is.

fields.name: largest single-bar move
fields.meaning: The biggest move in the generated window, a sharp drop.

fields.name: net move over the window
fields.meaning: Total change from the start of the window to the end.

fields.name: typical arrow size at the end
fields.meaning: How strongly the model still wanted to move the sample at the final step; small means it sits in a realistic region.

fields.name: arrow size of a real window checked
fields.meaning: The same measure on a real window; much bigger than 3 means that window looks unusual to the model.

example.reading: Use the generated window as a scenario, not a forecast. The arrow size is the useful diagnostic: values far above the typical ones flag windows that deserve a human look. Compare generated and real windows on volatility and tail size before using them in tests.
